runs.text: Critical thinking is best defined as:
Asking questions and seeking answers about a topic in order to develop a position on it
Finding all of the weaknesses in an argument
Finding all of the strengths in an argument
Arguing a specific point of view in front of an audience
Researching experts’ perspectives and arguments on a topic in order to develop a position on it

runs.text: True or False: a good conclusion restates your thesis and main ideas.

slides.notes: Optional review quiz. Brian: "If that’s not your gig, delete the slides." If you keep it, make it a game: read the question, take answers, then click to the reveal. Candy or other small prizes help. Answer: False. Restating can feel very repetitive. A good conclusion offers final reflection, arguments, or a call to action based on everything you just said.

runs.text: True or False: a good conclusion restates your thesis and main ideas.

slides.notes: The reveal. False. Restating can feel very repetitive. A good conclusion offers final reflection, arguments, or a call to action based on everything you just said.
Ah, the conclusion. So difficult and annoying for so many students, largely because we were all taught to restate the thesis and main ideas.

runs.text: restates the thesis and main ideas

slides.notes: Even if you were taught this (or taught it yourself), accept that it’s a bland, unimaginative ending. It makes sense for a speech or a sales pitch, where an audience retains a fraction of what they hear: "my floors look better, cost less, and are greener… so in conclusion, my floors are the best." A critical essay is on the page, for an intelligent reader who can reread.

runs.text: Restating your thesis and main ideas can make you seem like

slides.notes: "Yeah, man, I was there with you. I just read your whole essay, and now you’re repeating it to make sure I got it?"
Our conclusion paragraph does mark the end of the essay, but it’s more than an ending: it’s a deduction from everything we just said.

runs.text: By the end of your essay, you should have exhaustively defined, illustrated, and proven the elements of your thesis. And your reader should be right there with you. So if everything you just said is true, then
what deductions, or conclusions, can you draw from it all?

slides.notes: Let the class sit with the question for a moment before moving on.

runs.text: Rhetorical questions can create a nice
in a discussion or argument. For example, in the sample essay on education, Haley began her conclusion paragraph with the following…

slides.notes: Remind them what a rhetorical question really is: a question asked so the writer can supply the answer they want the reader to hear.

runs.text: How the sample essay’s conclusion begins
If we assume that teachers don’t like to be boring, then why doesn’t the education system teach them how to prioritize creative thinking in classrooms?
— Haley, “Bored in the USA” (read the conclusion together)

slides.notes: Read Haley’s whole conclusion together: a shared reference point for what comes next.

runs.text: Many a good conclusion begins with “Perhaps”
It’s assertive and smart without being aggressive, and it fits a conclusion’s tone:
With “perhaps,” you can offer ideas (even new ones) without new support. The support is already in your essay.

slides.notes: "Perhaps this… but maybe not. I’m just throwing it out there." Students may introduce a new idea here as food for thought on the way out; they don’t need to write a whole new essay about it.

runs.text: If we assume that teachers don’t like to be boring, then why doesn’t the education system teach them how to prioritize creative thinking in classrooms?
Perhaps the way teachers are taught today is wrong.
They put too much pressure on teachers to increase scores, and this trickles down to the students, and suddenly everything we do in school is about “the test.”

slides.notes: Haley hasn’t talked about how teachers are taught anywhere in her essay. It’s a new idea, offered as she exits. She could write a separate essay about it; she doesn’t have to. Really thoughtful.

runs.text: Supporting quote (if working with a text)
Final, concluding sentence: the big, final point

slides.notes: Five moves, in order. The question creates a shift; "Perhaps" lets students offer a deduction (even a new idea) confidently without having to prove it all over again; then two sentences of their own analysis, a quote if they have a text, and one big closing line.

runs.text: QUESTION AND BIG FINAL POINT IN COLOUR · “PERHAPS” HIGHLIGHTED
If we assume that teachers don’t like to be boring, then why doesn’t the education system teach them how to prioritize creative thinking in classrooms?
Perhaps the way teachers are taught today is wrong.

They put too much pressure on teachers to increase scores, and this trickles down to the students, and suddenly everything we do in school is about “the test.” No one can learn under those conditions. However, if administrators and teachers prioritized creative lessons, we could build engagement and excitement between the teachers and students.
Imagine the impact this could have on student learning and the teaching profession!

slides.notes: Walk the structure: the rhetorical question; the "perhaps"; a few sentences of opinion and reaction; the solution ("if administrators and teachers prioritized creative lessons…"), the antidote to everything she has argued; then the big final sentence. On the Critical Essay Form the conclusion is the upside-down funnel: specific back out to big. "Imagine the impact this could have on student learning and the teaching profession!"

runs.text: Walk them back through every room: “Remember the kitchen?”
Push them out a second-floor window and yell “Tour’s over!”
Take them out to the back deck, or back to the front door.
Point out the neighborhood, maybe a house next door you won’t visit. Then say a thoughtful goodbye.

slides.notes: You’ve toured them through the living room, the kitchen, the bedrooms. You wouldn’t scream and run away (what many students do), and you wouldn’t repeat the tour. Instead, a back deck: there’s a little bit more. Or the front door, pointing at the neighborhood: some ideas, even new ones, you acknowledge without exploring, placing your house in the greater neighborhood and world. Leave this slide up while students write.

elements.alt: The YAWP! editor on the Conclusion step.

runs.text: End on your big, final point

slides.notes: Today’s YAWP! editor on the Conclusion Paragraph step. This part usually goes fast: once body paragraphs are done they’re in the home stretch. As you work the room, watch the rhetorical questions. Some will be too simple or lead nowhere; help them find a relevant question that springboards their final thoughts. For many students this is the first conclusion like this they have ever built.
